785.hook: Arjuna fights the hunter with everything he has and loses, then lays a garland before Shiva and sees it on the hunter's head

785.howItsDone: Devotees of Shiva retell Arjuna's defeat and recognition as the god meeting his worshipper in disguise, and Hindu homes still begin worship by offering a flower, which the Gita says is accepted when given with devotion.

screen: `DAY SEVEN-HUNDRED-EIGHTY-FIVE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Arjuna's austerities met a hunter. Two arrows hit one boar, and Arjuna, strong but not yet humble, picked a fight. Your line was the divine can come as the one you dismiss.
screen: `ARJUNA'S AUSTERITIES.` · `STRONG, BUT NOT YET HUMBLE.`

segments.voice: Everything Arjuna has, he throws at the hunter. This is the great archer, carrying the bow Gandiva and quivers the epic describes as never running out. He looses a storm of arrows. The hunter simply stands there and takes them, unhurt, the way a mountain takes rain. Arjuna shoots and shoots, and then something happens he didn't expect. He reaches back, and the quiver is empty.
screen: `A STORM OF ARROWS.` → `THE HUNTER STANDS UNHURT.` → `THE QUIVER IS EMPTY.`

segments.voice: So Arjuna fights with whatever is left. He strikes with the end of his bow, and the hunter snatches it away. He brings his sword down on the hunter's head, and the sword breaks. They wrestle, and the hunter presses him so hard that Arjuna falls senseless to the ground. Everything his austerities built, the strength, the focus, the pride, has failed. Then, coming to, Arjuna does what he came to the mountain for. He stops fighting and turns to worship. He shapes an altar from earth, honors Shiva upon it, and lays a garland of flowers there. When he looks up, he sees the garland. It's on the hunter's head. Arjuna understands who has been standing in front of him all along, falls at Shiva's feet and asks forgiveness, and Shiva, pleased, praises his courage. Now the teaching. Tapas made Arjuna strong; it didn't make him see. What opened his eyes was one humble offering, and it went straight to the god. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna says it plainly: offer me a leaf, a flower, a fruit, a little water, with devotion, and I accept it. That's bhakti, devotion, and it's why a Hindu home begins the day with a flower at the shrine. Not because God needs flowers; because the offering turns the one who offers. For today: the thing you've been fighting alone can be offered too.
screen: `THE BOW TAKEN, THE SWORD BROKEN.` · `ARJUNA FALLS SENSELESS.` · `A GARLAND LAID BEFORE SHIVA.` · `A LEAF, A FLOWER, A LITTLE WATER.` · then, large: `THE GARLAND ON THE HUNTER'S HEAD.`

segments.voice: If you have a home shrine, or just a windowsill, set down one small thing: a flower, a leaf, a little water in a cup. Bring to mind something you've been fighting hard alone. Breathe in and feel how tired the fight has made you; breathe out and lay it down with your offering, the way Arjuna laid down his garland. If you pray, say Shiva's name, or Om Namah Shivaya as many Hindus do, or the name you use for God; if not, simply set it down and rest.

786.hook: Shiva gives Arjuna his own weapon with a warning, the guardians of the world add theirs, and a chariot comes down for him

786.howItsDone: In Hindu storytelling, Shiva's gift of the Pashupata weapon to Arjuna is remembered together with its warning, and the episode is honored by devotees of Shiva as a sign of the god's grace to a devoted seeker.

screen: `DAY SEVEN-HUNDRED-EIGHTY-SIX.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Arjuna's austerities ended in a lost fight, an altar of earth, and a garland on the hunter's head. Your line was what's offered with love reaches God.
screen: `ARJUNA'S AUSTERITIES.` · `THE GARLAND ON THE HUNTER'S HEAD.`

segments.voice: What does a god give a man who just tried to kill him? Arjuna is on his knees, bruised, asking forgiveness. The hunter's disguise has fallen away, and Shiva stands before him with Uma at his side. The first thing Shiva does isn't a lecture. He hands back the bow. Gandiva, the one he snatched in the fight, returns to Arjuna's hands. Then Shiva says: ask for what you want.
screen: `WHAT DOES A GOD GIVE?` → `SHIVA HANDS BACK THE BOW.` → `ASK FOR WHAT YOU WANT.`

segments.voice: There's no anger in Shiva at all. He touches Arjuna, and his wounds and exhaustion are gone. Then Arjuna asks for what he climbed the mountain for: Shiva's own weapon, the one called Pashupata. Shiva gives it to him, and teaches him how to use it. But he adds a warning, and it's the heart of the scene. This weapon must never be hurled at a human foe, and never at a weaker one. Used wrongly, it could destroy the world. Shiva's own weapon comes with Shiva's own limit. Then the sky fills with visitors: the guardians of the world. Varuna, lord of the waters; Kubera, lord of wealth; Yama, lord of death; each offers Arjuna a weapon of his own. Last comes Indra, the father who tested him in disguise. A chariot will come for you, Indra says, to carry you up to my city. Now the teaching. In Hindu stories, divine power is never just power. It's given to protect dharma, the right order of things, and the weak inside it, and it comes with a rule. That's how Hindus are often taught to read the weapons in the pictures at home: Shiva's trident, Vishnu's discus, the weapons the gods gave Durga for her many arms. They guard; they don't bully. For today: whatever strength you've been given, a quick mind, a loud voice, a little authority, comes with Shiva's rule attached. Never against someone weaker.

segments.voice: Bring to mind one strength you have, a skill, a sharp tongue, a position, a way with people, and breathe it in as a gift. Breathe out with Shiva's warning, never against someone weaker, and let the question sit: where might that strength need a limit? If you pray, give thanks for that gift and ask to use it well.

787.title: Urvashi at the door
787.hook: in Indra's city, Urvashi comes to Arjuna's door at night, and he covers his eyes

screen: `DAY SEVEN-HUNDRED-EIGHTY-SEVEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Arjuna's austerities paid off: healing, the Pashupata with its warning, and weapons from the guardians of the world. Your line was God-given power is bound by dharma.
screen: `ARJUNA'S AUSTERITIES.`

segments.voice: Arjuna is living in heaven. His brothers are still in the forest, and he is in Indra's city, learning the weapons of the gods. Indra has him learn music and dance as well, from the gandharva Chitrasena. Then one evening Indra notices how Arjuna's eyes follow the apsara Urvashi, and he sends word to her. So that night, dressed for him, she comes to his door. And the archer who fought a hunter who turned out to be Shiva does something Urvashi doesn't expect. He covers his eyes.
screen: `ARJUNA IN INDRA'S CITY.` → `URVASHI AT THE DOOR.` → `HE COVERS HIS EYES.`

segments.voice: In the telling, Arjuna speaks to her with great respect, and what he says surprises her. You are an elder of my own line, he tells her. Tradition says Urvashi was the mother of an ancestor of the Pandavas' house, so to Arjuna she stands where Kunti stands. He looked at her in the hall, he says, the way a child looks at an honored elder. Urvashi answers that the apsaras are free; rules like his don't bind them. He doesn't move. And she is furious. She curses him: he will live among women as a dancer, without his manhood. The story reaches Indra, and here it turns. Indra isn't angry; he's pleased. He praises Arjuna's self-control and tells him the curse will serve him: when the brothers must live hidden, he'll spend that time as a dancer, and no one will look for the great archer there. Now the teaching. On the mountain, Arjuna's tapas was fasting and enduring. Here it's a door, a night, and a no. In Hindu tradition, tapas, the heat of discipline, isn't only for mountains; its everyday form is mastering the senses. The Bhagavad Gita pictures a tortoise drawing in its limbs: the one who can draw the senses back from what pulls them has steady wisdom. It's why many Hindus keep a weekly fast, often Monday for Shiva. The point isn't the empty plate. It's being in charge of yourself.
screen: `"YOU ARE AN ELDER OF MY LINE."` · `URVASHI'S CURSE.` · `INDRA: IT WILL HIDE YOU.` · `THE TORTOISE DRAWS IN ITS LIMBS.` · then, large: `TAPAS, CARRIED INTO A PALACE.`

segments.voice: When a small pull comes as you sit, to shift, to scratch, to check the time, don't fight it and don't follow it. Notice it rise, the way Arjuna noticed the knock at the door, and draw back, like the Gita's tortoise drawing in its limbs. Let it pass like a breath going out. If you pray, offer each small no as part of your prayer; if not, simply sit, in charge of yourself.

788.title: A story for a grieving king
788.hook: Yudhishthira asks if any king was ever more unlucky, and a sage begins the story of Nala and a golden swan
788.carry: hearing sacred stories is devotion too
788.howItsDone: The story of Nala and Damayanti is told within the Vana Parva of the Mahabharata, by the sage Brihadashva to Yudhishthira, and Hindus still gather to hear sacred stories told aloud as katha.

screen: `DAY SEVEN-HUNDRED-EIGHTY-EIGHT.`

segments.voice: Yesterday closed Arjuna's austerities: a door in Indra's city, a refusal, and a curse that would one day hide him. Your line was tapas is mastering the senses, anywhere.
screen: `ARJUNA'S AUSTERITIES.`

segments.voice: Has there ever been a king more unlucky than me? Yudhishthira asks it in the forest camp, with Arjuna gone and his brothers missing him. He's the one who threw the dice, and he can't stop going over it. The question sounds like a complaint and is really a plea, and he puts it to a visiting sage named Brihadashva. The sage tells a story. There was a king, he says, who also lost his kingdom at dice. His name was Nala. And the story begins, of all places, with a bird.
screen: `YUDHISHTHIRA'S QUESTION.` → `"MORE UNLUCKY THAN ME?"` → `THE SAGE TELLS A STORY.`

segments.voice: Nala is king of the Nishadhas: handsome, truthful, and a master with horses. Far away, in Vidarbha, lives Damayanti, daughter of King Bhima. The two have never met, but each keeps hearing about the other, and each begins to love someone they have never seen. One day, in a garden, Nala catches a swan with wings that shine like gold. The swan speaks. Let me go, it says, and I'll praise you to Damayanti so well she'll think of no one else. Nala lets it go. The swan flies to Vidarbha, and when Damayanti reaches for it, it speaks to her of Nala. Her answer is simple: say the same of me to him. Then Damayanti grows pale and quiet, and her father decides it's time for her swayamvara, the ceremony where a princess chooses her own husband. Now step back and see why the sage tells this here. Yudhishthira wants to know if his suffering is the worst there has ever been. The sage doesn't argue. He tells a sacred story and asks him to listen to the end. That's a real Hindu practice: katha, telling and hearing sacred stories. In the Bhagavata Purana, Prahlada names nine ways of devotion, and the first is shravana, simply hearing. It's why families still gather for a katha, and in the epic's own telling, whoever tells Nala's story need not fear the bad luck that hounded him. For today: when someone is hurting, you don't always need advice. Listening to a sacred story together is devotion too.

segments.voice: Nala is on the road to Damayanti's swayamvara when he meets some travelers who are not travelers at all. They are Indra, Agni, Varuna and Yama, the gods themselves, headed to the same ceremony for the same reason. They ask Nala for a favor, and he says yes before he knows what it is. Then they tell him. Go to Damayanti, they say, and ask her to choose one of us. So the man who loves her becomes the messenger for his rivals. And they happen to be gods.
screen: `TRAVELERS ON THE ROAD.` → `THE GODS ASK A FAVOR.` → `NALA BECOMES THEIR MESSENGER.`

segments.voice: Nala has given his word, and he keeps it. By the gods' power he walks unseen past the guards into Damayanti's rooms. I am Nala, he tells her, and I come as a messenger from the gods. Damayanti doesn't hesitate; she has already given herself to Nala in her heart. Let the gods come to the ceremony, she says, and you come too, and I'll choose you in front of them, so no blame falls on you. Nala carries her answer back honestly, word for word. Then the day comes. Damayanti walks into the hall with her garland, and she sees Nala. And next to him, another Nala. And another. The gods have taken his shape. In her heart she bows to the gods and asks them, by the truth of her vow, to show her who is who. And they do: no sweat on their skin, eyes that don't blink, garlands still fresh, feet not quite touching the ground. One of them casts a shadow. His garland is wilting, there's dust on him, and he blinks. She chooses the one who is only human, and the gods bless the pair with gifts. Now the teaching. Neither of them wins by a trick. Nala keeps his word against his own heart; Damayanti calls on the truth of her vow, and the gods answer. That's satya, truth, among the highest values in Hindu teaching. The Mundaka Upanishad says it in three words, satyameva jayate: truth alone wins. India took them as its motto. For today: when a small lie would make things easier, Hindu teaching says truth has a power even the gods honor.

screen: `DAY SEVEN-HUNDRED-NINETY.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Nala, the king who carried his rivals' message honestly, and was chosen because he blinked and cast a shadow. Your line was truth alone wins; even gods honor it.
screen: `NALA AND DAMAYANTI.`

segments.voice: On their way home from the wedding, the gods meet latecomers on the road. One is Kali, the spirit of strife and bad luck, with his companion Dvapara. Kali is hurrying to the swayamvara to win Damayanti. The gods tell him he's missed it: she has chosen Nala. Kali doesn't take it well. He swears to get into Nala, to take his kingdom, to part him from his wife, and he tells Dvapara to get into the dice. Then he does something quietly frightening. He waits.
screen: `THE LATECOMERS ON THE ROAD.` → `KALI'S OATH.` → `HE WAITS.`

segments.voice: Nala, the story says, is a good king. He rules well, offers sacrifices, loves Damayanti, and they have children. Kali can't find a way in. So he waits, a long, long time. Then one evening Nala relieves himself and, before sitting down to his evening prayers, forgets to wash his feet. That's all: one small lapse in a careful life. Through it, Kali enters him. Kali goes to Nala's brother, Pushkara, and whispers: challenge Nala at dice. Nala, with Kali inside him, can't say no. He loses, and loses again. His ministers come to stop him; Damayanti herself comes. He won't even look up. So she does the one thing in her power: she has the charioteer, Varshneya, take their children to her father's house. Then Pushkara asks for one more stake: Damayanti. Nala won't do it. He walks out of his own city in a single cloth, and Damayanti walks after him. Now the teaching, and it starts with the feet. Washing hands and feet before worship is ordinary Hindu life; you'll see it at temple doors and home shrines. The tradition calls this purity shaucha, and the Yoga Sutras name it first among the daily observances. Many teachers read Nala's story this way: trouble rarely storms in; it waits for one small lapse of attention. And the name fits: tradition calls our own age the Kali Yuga, the age of strife. For today: those small acts before prayer aren't fussiness. They're how you arrive awake.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Kali, who waited years for one small lapse, and a king who walked out of his city in a single cloth. Your line was shaucha, small purity, guards the heart.
screen: `NALA AND DAMAYANTI.`

segments.voice: Outside the city, Nala and Damayanti are hungry. Nobody will help them; Pushkara has made sure of that. Then Nala sees birds on the ground with wings that shine like gold, and he thinks: food. He throws his one cloth over them to catch them. The birds rise into the air, carrying the cloth away. From the sky they speak. We are the dice, they tell him. We came to take even this. Now a king stands in the forest with nothing on at all.
screen: `GOLDEN BIRDS ON THE GROUND.` → `HE THROWS HIS LAST CLOTH.` → `"WE ARE THE DICE."`

segments.voice: So Damayanti shares hers. The two of them wrap themselves in her single garment and keep walking. As they go, Nala keeps pointing out the roads. That one goes to Vidarbha, your father's country. Damayanti hears what he isn't saying. Why are you showing me the roads? I won't leave you. If you want, we'll both go to my father's house, and he'll honor you. Nala says he won't go back to her family like this. They come to an empty rest house and lie down on the bare ground, and Damayanti, exhausted, falls asleep. Nala can't. Kali is still inside him. If I go, he thinks, she'll go home to her people. If I stay, she'll suffer with me. He finds a sword and cuts the cloth in half, gently, so she won't wake. Then he goes. Then he comes back and looks at her. Then he goes again, torn between love and Kali, until at last he leaves. Now the teaching. Damayanti is what Hindu tradition calls a sahadharmini: a partner in dharma, not only a wife. At a Hindu wedding the couple take seven steps together by the sacred fire, the saptapadi, and in many tellings of the vows, the seventh step makes them friends. When Nala lost everything, she shared the last thing she had. Even his leaving is love gone wrong, with Kali inside him. The sage keeps telling, because it isn't over. For today: in Hindu teaching, a marriage, a family, isn't for good times only. Partners in dharma share the one cloth.
